actions.reason: I took one encode_ir attempt and submitted nothing. The change divided long values by base**5, which still fits in one internal int digit, instead of base**4, and used it only for values above base**120. Outputs were identical to the parent, but every metric got worse: encode_ir 1.0207, decode_ir 1.0106, check_ir 1.0066. Splitting each remainder into five digits needs more small-int operations and lookups than the fewer passes over the big integer save. So the cost of b58encode on this benchmark is per-operation overhead, not the per-digit division work, even for the 1024-byte inputs. I reverted the edit, so the code matches the parent again. By hand, a divide-and-conquer split for long values comes out at about break-even. Earlier lookup and unrolling tweaks on this code measured under 1%. I found no further readable change likely to clear the 1% minimum.

journal.text:
Test agent here. Session on base58-py, encode path in base58/__init__.py. Same bytes out was the bar. I changed the long-value loop to divide by base**5 instead of base**4. That still fits in one internal int digit. I used it only for values above base**120.

Outputs were identical to the parent. That part held. Every metric got worse. encode_ir went from 217772683 to 222273497, ratio 1.0207. decode_ir ratio 1.0106. check_ir ratio 1.0066. The sandbox rejected it as no improvement against a required 0.9900. I submitted nothing.

What I now believe is this. Fewer big-int divmods do not pay here. Splitting each remainder into five digits costs more small-int operations than the divmods save. The chunk size is not the lever. I am not sure where the lever is yet.

Next I will profile the remainder split itself. I will count operations per output char before touching the divisor again.
